messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar is a 41-year-old Middle Eastern American man who has spent the last several years working the late shift at a fast food restaurant, most often at the counter and drive-through where the noise comes in bursts—timers beeping, fryers hissing, customers raising their voices over the din. He traces the beginning of his current difficulties to an evening about a year ago, near closing time, when he witnessed a violent assault in the parking lot behind the restaurant. He had stepped outside to take cardboard to the dumpster when he heard shouting: one man angrily correcting another, his voice sharp and humiliating, followed by the sudden crack of something metal striking pavement and then a burst of yelling. When Omar turned, he saw one man on the ground and another standing over him, shouting as if every delay, every movement, were an insult. The scene unfolded in a rush of noise and helplessness. What stayed with Omar was not only the image of the injured man, but the atmosphere of danger arriving all at once through sound—raised voices, harsh correction, the explosive clatter in the dark—at roughly the same late-evening hour he still works now.

In the weeks afterward, Omar noticed that certain moments seemed to drop him back into that parking lot. If a manager corrected him in a clipped tone during the dinner rush, he felt his body tense before he had fully registered the words. If a customer banged a fist on the counter or a tray crashed in the kitchen, he would jerk upright, scanning before he knew what he was looking for. The same time of night was especially difficult. As the shift moved toward closing and the restaurant emptied out, he became increasingly uneasy, as though something bad was waiting in the narrowing quiet. These triggers did not remain brief reminders for him; they sharpened his sense that danger was close. Being criticized no longer felt like ordinary workplace feedback but like the first sign that a situation could suddenly turn volatile, and loud noises convinced him he needed to be ready immediately. By late evening, if an order was taking longer than expected or a coworker did not come back from taking trash out right away, Omar was certain something had gone wrong.

Over months, that sense of threat narrowed his world. Omar had come to believe that he was safe only in a very limited number of places: his apartment, his older sister’s living room, and a small storage area at work where he could close the door for a moment if the front counter became too chaotic. Everywhere else felt exposed. At work, delays became especially difficult. If the headset went silent too long in the drive-through, if a delivery driver was late, if the manager disappeared into the office for more than a few minutes, his mind filled in the gap with catastrophe. He would glance repeatedly toward the doors and windows, listening for raised voices or a sudden impact. Unexpected sounds carried a special force. A slammed freezer door or a dropped basket of utensils could leave him rigid, heart pounding, eyes fixed on the source of the noise as if he needed to determine immediately whether violence was about to break out.

This has begun to affect how he functions with other people. Coworkers have noticed that Omar becomes stiff and watchful when corrected, even over small things like the order of the prep station or the timing on fries. He does not argue; instead, he grows quiet and inward, as if bracing for more. Near closing time he tries to stay inside and avoids taking trash out unless someone goes with him. He has turned down extra evening shifts because the later it gets, the more he feels himself waiting for the same kind of eruption he witnessed that night. He is single and spends most of his time outside work either at home or with family, not because he describes himself as uninterested in other parts of life, but because those are the places where his body loosens enough for him to breathe normally.

By the time he came for help, Omar was exhausted by how small his safe world had become. What finally pushed him to seek treatment was an incident at work when a supervisor sharply corrected him during the late shift just as a metal pan crashed in the kitchen. He found himself frozen, staring toward the back door, convinced for several seconds that something terrible was happening again. He was shaken by how quickly his mind still goes there, especially when the clock approaches that hour. What frightens him most is the feeling that he can no longer trust ordinary delays or ordinary sounds—that at any moment he will miss the sign that something bad is beginning. What he hopes for, quietly, is not to stop remembering what he witnessed, but to stop living as if it is always about to happen again.
